content: The mandibular second molar is a tooth located distally, meaning it is positioned farther away from the midline of the face compared to the mandibular first molars. However, it is mesial, or closer to the midline, relative to the mandibular third molars. This arrangement applies only to permanent teeth. In deciduous (baby) teeth, the mandibular second molar is the last tooth in the mouth, as there is no third molar present behind it. The primary function of the mandibular second molar, like all molars, is to grind food during mastication (chewing). This grinding action is its principal role in the process of breaking down food. While there is more variation in the anatomy of the mandibular second molar compared to the first mandibular molar, the second molar typically has four cusps. These cusps are distributed as two on the buccal (cheek-facing) side and two on the lingual (tongue-facing) side. There are significant differences between deciduous mandibular molars and permanent mandibular molars, despite their similar functions. It is important to note that permanent mandibular molars do not have any preceding teeth in the dental arch. In contrast, deciduous molars, despite being called molars, are eventually replaced by permanent premolars. In the universal system of dental notation, deciduous mandibular second molars are designated by uppercase letters. The right deciduous mandibular second molar is labeled as T, while the left one is labeled as K. In the international system of dental notation, a different numbering system is used. The right deciduous mandibular second molar is identified as 85, and the left one is identified as 75. For permanent mandibular second molars, the universal system of notation assigns numbers. The right permanent mandibular second molar is designated as 31, and the left one is designated as 18. These designations are widely used in dental practice for identification and communication purposes.
